title: The racehorse (29–32)
hookLine: awake among the sleeping, the wise move on like a racehorse leaving a nag behind

cards: There's a particular quiet at five in the morning. The house is asleep. The street is asleep.
Even the phone is quiet, because everyone who might send a message is asleep too. People up at that hour, for a flight or a baby or a shift, sometimes call it a secret extra room in the day.
In some monasteries the bell rings in that room, well before dawn, for sitting and chanting while the town sleeps. The Dhammapada has a picture for someone awake while others sleep.

teach.b: Verse twenty-nine, in Müller's English: “Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.” A racer and a hack: a fast racehorse and a tired old nag.
The commentary tells it about two monks who went to the forest together for the rains. One gathered firewood, sat by the fire in the evenings, and chatted with the young novices half the night.

The other kept to his practice, sitting and walking, and slept only in the middle watch. By the end of the rains the second had awakened. When they came back, the chatty monk told the Buddha his friend had been lazy.
The Buddha said it was the other way around, and spoke the verse. The friend by the fire was the nag. Careful, though: the verse isn't praising people who sleep four hours and brag about it.
Awake in the Dhammapada mostly means inwardly awake: heedful, present, not drifting. Same forest, same hours. One spent them drifting; one spent them awake.
The chapter closes with three more verses.
Heedfulness, it says, raised the god Indra to lordship among the gods. The heedful monk moves like a fire, burning up his fetters, small and large.

And someone who delights in heedfulness can't fall away; they're close to nibbana. So, chapter two: the path of the deathless, an island, and now the racehorse. One word, heedfulness, seen three ways.

how: Some Buddhist monasteries rise well before dawn for sitting and chanting, and some lay practitioners keep a short sitting early in the morning before the household wakes.

o: a horse that runs for prize money at the races
someone who rushes through life to win every contest
the heedful one, awake inside, who moves ahead of the drifters

games.q: match the pieces of verses twenty-nine to thirty-two.
p: the tired old horse left behind
moves like a fire, burning fetters

s: verse twenty-nine praises sleeping as little as possible
'awake' here mostly means inwardly awake: heedful, not drifting.
in the commentary, the chatty monk accused his friend of being lazy
the Buddha said it was the other way around.
the chapter says heedfulness raised the god Indra to lordship among the gods
verse thirty uses Indra, called Maghavan, as an example.

games.q: you're the Buddha. a monk back from the forest says his companion was lazy all rains, while he himself kept the fire going and talked with the novices. what do you say?
o: praise him for his hard work.
say it was the other way around: he was the tired horse.
send them both back to the forest.
games.why: the Buddha told him his friend had been the racehorse and he the hack, and spoke verse twenty-nine.

practice: Picture the house very early, before anyone is up: no messages, no noise, just you, the dark window, maybe the first birds. Let that stillness be here now, even if it's the middle of the afternoon.
Feel what it's like to be awake while the world is quiet: the breath, the body, the room.

wordCard.voice: The racehorse. The heedful one, awake among the sleepers, moving on like a racer leaving the tired horse behind.

orig.note: Pali: wakeful, from verse twenty-nine's 'bahujagaro,' very wakeful among the sleepers.

carryVoice: Your line: awake among the sleeping. Awake inside, whatever the hour on the clock. Chapter two, finished.

sources.q: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 30–32; Dhammapada-atthakatha, story of the two companion monks (verse 29)
